batch_strategy: Measure local solvent-ratio brackets and loading contrasts around graph-specific response transitions, with compact structural controls to constrain transfer of late-retention corrections.

choices.reason: m125 at 5/1 and 50 uL tests the low-amount side of a measured late-finish regime. Existing 100 uL measurements also differ with recorded DCM volume; this label helps distinguish amount dependence from unresolved variation in the response.
m198 at 20/1 and 150 uL provides an amount contrast to its measured 50 uL condition. The existing 10/1-to-20/1 response rises strongly; this point tests whether that rise transfers to higher loading.

m212, a secondary amine, at 5/1 and 100 uL fills an intermediate point between measured moderate 2/1 retention and much later 10/1 retention. It can teach the location of a steep basic-compound response.

m141 at 2/1 and 50 uL completes a low-amount bracket between measured 1/1 and 5/1 conditions. This sterically substituted pyridine offers a useful test of amount-sensitive onset versus finish responses.

m160 at 1/1 and 50 uL adds a low-amount anchor before the large measured retention increase at 5/1. It helps locate the transition in an amino nitrile without assuming that all donor-containing graphs respond alike.
m161 at 2/1 and 100 uL fills the amount gap between its measured 50 and 150 uL rows. Comparison with the positional amino nitrile m160 can constrain structure-dependent transition behavior.

m211 at 1/1 and 150 uL tests the compact side of its basic-ring response against measured 100 uL behavior. This supplies a boundary constraint so corrections from its late PE-rich rows do not spread into stronger mobile phases.

m73 at 5/1 and approximately 100 uL brackets unusual measured 1/1 records and compact-onset weaker-solvent records. Some measured endpoint ordering is inconsistent, so this tests whether the apparent feature extends beyond those isolated rows.

m73 at 10/1 and approximately 100 uL pairs with the selected 5/1 point to map the region beyond its unusual 1/1 records. The pair can delimit a localized feature without treating the anomalous endpoint ordering as established chemistry.

m100 at 5/1 and 150 uL fills a fixed-amount ratio gap between measured compact 1/1 behavior and a later 20/1 finish. Its measured pure-EA row also has an early onset and wider interval, making separate endpoint learning useful.

m6 at 50/1 and 150 uL tests amount transfer after the measured 50 uL benzodioxole row disproved a much later acquisition-time prediction. The current prediction is more compact; this tests whether that correction holds at higher amount.

m177 at 50/1 and 50 uL extends the measured 100-versus-150 uL contrast, whose finishes differ dramatically while onsets remain early. This lower-amount point discriminates a loading association from a broadly late graph response.

m177 at 10/1 and 100 uL fills the amount gap between measured 50 and 150 uL rows with substantially different finishes. Together with the selected 50/1 point, it constrains the amount-by-ratio interaction.

m186 at 1/1 and 100 uL extends the recent pure-EA label at the same amount and DCM volume. It tests whether the unexpectedly broad pure-EA finish persists at the neighboring ratio while onset remains early.

m58 at 10/1 and 50 uL extends an accurately predicted measured 5/1 point toward the much later measured 50/1 regime. It probes where onset and finish begin to increase for this ortho-substituted phenol.

m135 at 10/1 and 50 uL supplies a low-amount contrast to its measured 100 uL late condition. The compact pure-EA and intermediate 5/1 observations make this useful for separating solvent response from amount effects in a benzyl alcohol.

m119 at 0/1 and 150 uL anchors a fixed-amount curve that is measured at 2/1 and 5/1. The latter conditions rise sharply in both endpoints; this tests the strong-solvent baseline for the same donor-containing graph.

m117 at 1/1 and 100 uL fills an amount gap relative to the measured 150 uL row at the same 600 uL DCM volume. Paired with its selected 2/1 row, it tests the predicted finish decrease without confounding amount or loading-solvent volume.

m117 at 2/1 and 100 uL is predicted to finish earlier than the selected 1/1 condition. Measuring both at fixed loading tests whether this local nonmonotonic response is reproducible or a model interpolation artifact.

m207 at 0/1 and 150 uL provides a strong-solvent anchor for a graph with much later measured 10/1 behavior. It helps localize the late response rather than applying a uniform alcohol correction across ratios.
m207 at 10/1 and 150 uL tests whether the measured late response at 100 uL persists at higher amount. The selected pure-EA point provides a fixed-amount ratio contrast for the same graph.

m204 at 1/1 and 150 uL supplies the high-amount baseline before its measured 5/1 and 10/1 retention increases. It also compares with the measured 100 uL 1/1 row, helping separate amount effects from a steep ratio response.

m150 at 0/1 and 50 uL anchors the compact, zero-HBA halogenated-aromatic region at low amount. This control constrains transfer of late polar-compound corrections to a graph lacking conventional hydrogen-bonding groups.

m151 at 50/1 and 50 uL contrasts with the measured 100 uL row at the same ratio. This chloroiodoarene supplies a compact weak-solvent control for distinguishing loading effects from changes associated with polar functional groups.
m152 at 1/1 and 150 uL extends measured high-amount 2/1 behavior and a measured low-amount 1/1 condition. It constrains amount transfer in a heavy halogenated aryl ether that has remained compact.

m153 at 5/1 and 150 uL fills a ratio gap near measured compact 2/1 behavior. Comparison with selected related aryl ethers tests whether their low-retention response transfers across substitution patterns.

m154 at 20/1 and 100 uL provides an amount contrast to the recently measured 150 uL condition, which remained compact. It helps constrain loading corrections within the related halogenated aryl-ether family.
m69 at 1/1 and 100 uL fills the amount gap between measured compact 50 and 150 uL rows. It anchors an ordinary aryl alkyl ketone response against broader multifunctional-carbonyl examples.

m26 at 5/1 and 50 uL tests whether the broad measured 100 uL interval persists at lower amount. It supplies a beta-diketone comparison where finish changes can be learned separately from the near-early onset.

m168 at 0/1 and 100 uL adds a strong-solvent baseline for a diaryl beta-diketone whose measured PE-rich rows retain early onset with broader finishes. It constrains structural transfer among multifunctional carbonyl graphs.

m183 at 10/1 and 150 uL extends the measured 50 uL condition at the same ratio. This tests amount sensitivity in an aliphatic aldehyde environment and provides a comparison with aromatic aldehyde response curves.

m16 at 50/1 and 100 uL extends the measured 20/1 condition at fixed amount and PE loading solvent. It tests the high-PE response of a hydrophobic acrylate ester, providing a boundary comparison to more strongly retained multifunctional esters.

hypotheses.content: Solvent-ratio responses are graph-specific and can change V1 and V2 differently. Some graphs retain early onset while their finish shifts substantially, so a shared endpoint correction is inadequate.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Fixed-amount ratio brackets can teach separate onset and finish responses across chemically distinct graphs and reduce inappropriate smoothing of interval shape.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Which selected intermediate ratios show smooth endpoint changes, and which reveal a local dip, threshold, or primarily finish-driven response?

hypotheses.content: Endpoint differences associated with recorded sample amount and loading-solvent volume depend on ratio and molecular graph. Large finish differences in some families do not justify a universal loading shift; their causal mechanism remains unresolved.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Matched amount contrasts can supervise conditional loading effects and distinguish them from solvent-ratio interpolation. They also help expose variability that the recorded features may not explain.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the intermediate or lower-amount points reproduce the observed finish contrasts, and do compact aryl ethers show much smaller effects under comparable changes?

hypotheses.content: Some apparent aromatic retention peaks or weak-solvent delays are localized model failures or unusual records. Nearby condition labels are needed before treating them as transferable response features.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Local brackets and compact controls can delimit anomalous behavior and prevent isolated labels or extrapolation errors from distorting predictions for neighboring rows.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the new m73 ratio points support an extended response feature, and does the corrected compact m6 prediction persist at higher amount?

hypotheses.content: Functional-group arrangement and structural environment strongly affect joint onset and finish behavior. Hydrogen-bond donor counts, acceptor counts, or molecular mass alone cannot determine whether a graph enters a late-retention regime.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Related compact controls constrain where corrections from severe basic or multifunctional failures should transfer, improving the graph encoder's structure-condition discrimination.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the selected halogenated aryl ethers and hydrophobic carbonyl controls remain compact while the donor-containing response curves change substantially?

hypotheses.content: Certain basic or donor-containing families exhibit steep retention increases over limited solvent-ratio ranges. The transition location may be graph-specific; a sharp threshold is a useful hypothesis rather than an established universal mechanism.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Labels on both sides of steep response regions can improve interpolation and help the predictor distinguish a genuine ratio transition from an amount-dependent shift.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do intermediate ratios and matched amount contrasts locate reproducible steep transitions within each selected family?

feedback_interpretation: Recent outcomes weakened broad extrapolation rules. The m6 50/1 measurement was much more compact than its acquisition-time prediction; the current prediction has moved toward that result, so the selected higher-amount condition tests transfer of the correction rather than presuming a persistent residual. The m73 20/1 outcome also weakened the predicted late response, while its unusual 1/1 records still require local brackets and include inconsistent endpoint ordering. Conversely, m186 in pure EA had a substantially later finish than predicted despite early onset, showing that strong mobile phase does not guarantee a narrow interval. Accurate recent m109 and m58 results and compact m135, m152, and m154 outcomes argue against universal donor, mass, or loading shifts. Earlier m177 and m125 contrasts remain strong evidence for conditional finish sensitivity, although missing experimental variables and row variability limit causal interpretation. Historical errors are acquisition-time evidence, not current-model residuals.
batch_rationale: The 32 distinct candidate-table IDs combine condition exploration with targeted failure repair. The m73 and m117 pairs test local response shape; m177 supplies two informative amount-by-ratio contrasts; m207 supplies a fixed-amount ratio comparison. Additional basic, donor-containing, and carbonyl rows constrain transition boundaries, while halogenated aryl ethers, zero-HBA aromatics, and an ordinary aryl alkyl ketone anchor compact responses. Repeated graphs are used where their conditions create interpretable comparisons. Most selected molecules already have measured references, so the learning opportunity is improved structure-condition interpolation and transfer across the Row-distribution rather than molecular novelty. Quantile widths are secondary diagnostics, not calibrated epistemic uncertainty, and elution interval width is treated as a target property. This combination may improve both common compact predictions and the less frequent, high-loss late-finish regimes without forcing one global retention correction.
